content.text: Minimal APIs don't guess where a parameter comes from: they apply a fixed list of rules, and the parameter's name and type decide the result. When the rules pick a source you didn't mean, you get an empty 400 or a 500 on every endpoint, with no compiler warning.
aren't decoration; they change where the value is read from.
A teammate renames a route parameter from
because it reads better in the OpenAPI document. The handler still says
. The build is clean, no analyzer complains, and in production
starts answering 400 with an empty body. At the default log level, nothing is logged. The parameter didn't vanish: it quietly moved from the route to the query string, where nobody sends it.
The belief: minimal APIs look at each handler and figure out where every parameter should come from. Attributes like
are there for readability or documentation, and leaving them out changes nothing.
Most of the time, that's exactly what you see.
on a POST reads the JSON body. A registered service arrives from
without any attribute. The official samples rarely use attributes, so it's easy to conclude the framework is smart enough to always work it out.
in minimal APIs isn't inference in the "figure out what you meant" sense. It's a short, ordered list of rules, and the first rule that matches wins.
For each parameter, ASP.NET Core takes the first source that applies:

Controller habits make this one worse. In MVC, model binding fills a complex object property by property from the query string. Minimal APIs don't do that for a plain parameter;

blocks.title: One bad handler breaks every endpoint

content.text: A parameter the rules can't place doesn't fail the build or the startup. The app logs "Application started", then every request, health checks included, gets a 500 until the handler is fixed. A deployment that only waits for the process to start will look fine until its first request.

items.title: Make one request in your tests

content.text: An integration test that sends any request through the app builds every endpoint, so a parameter the rules can't place fails the test instead of the first production call.

items.text: Minimal APIs bind parameters with an ordered list of rules: attribute, special type,
, route-or-query for simple types, services, then the body.
A simple parameter is read from the route only if its name matches the template; otherwise it's read from the query string.
Headers and forms are never inferred, and complex types fall through to the body, which GET and DELETE don't allow implicitly.
